criteria.says: Given a policy's details, when the person presses the support button, then the support rule's details open.
Given a policy's details, when the person presses the category button, then the category's details open.

title: Walk a product's versions and parent in product details
what: A person opens a child revision or the parent product in the product details window.
why: It lets people move through a product's versions.

criteria.says: Given product details with child revisions, when a child is double-clicked, then it shows in the same window; with nothing selected nothing happens.
Given product details with a parent, when the person presses the parent button, then the parent shows in the same window.
Given the window resizes, when the list changes size, then the Name column fills the list beside Version.

title: Open products and nested rules from support rule details
what: A person opens a product or a nested support rule from the entries in support rule details.
why: It lets people follow which products a rule matches.

criteria.says: Given support rule entries, when one is double-clicked, then a product entry opens product details and a nested support rule shows in the same window; a missing product or no selection does nothing.
Given the window resizes, when the list changes size, then the Name column fills the list beside the version columns.

title: Inspect a policy's definition and its semantic policy text
what: A person inspects a policy's registry value, client extension, presentation and elements, copies a line, and opens the policy details. The person also reads the policy, with its comment and option values, as semantic policy text.
why: Administrators need to see how a template defines a policy.

terms.name: Inspector
terms.means: The window listing a policy's definition as written in the template; not the editor of its settings.

terms.name: Semantic policy text
terms.means: A text script describing a policy's state and options; not a registry file.

criteria.says: Given the inspector, when the person presses Ctrl+C, then the selected line is copied only if a line is selected.
Given a policy, when inspected, then a "Registry value" line shows only if it names a registry value and a "Client extension" line only if it names one.
Given choice elements, when inspected, then display names resolve through the file defining the policy and choices are numbered from zero in file order.
Given a list element, when inspected, then it states "User provides value names", a prefix, or "No prefix (values named for their data)".

Given affected registry settings with no on or off setting, when inspected, then it reads "Left implicit" if the policy names a registry value, "Left to elements" if not; inside a Yes/No element always "Left implicit".
Given a policy with a presentation and elements, when inspected, then presentation details list, each item with an ID matched to the element with that ID; items without an ID show none.
Given the inspector, when the person presses the details button, then the policy details open.

Given a policy, when shown, then there is one section per area it applies to, the machine section from the computer source and comments, the user section from the user source; an uncovered area is left out.
Given a section, when shown, then the comment is included only when one is stored, and option values only when the policy is Enabled.
Given a policy line, when written, then it starts with 'C' for a machine policy or 'U' for a user policy followed by the identifier.

Given values, when written, then whole numbers have a leading #, unsigned numbers are digits, yes/no is True or False, text is single-quoted, an empty list is 'None', text lists are bracketed with double-quoted items, tables bracketed with name: value lines.
Given a comment, when written, then backslashes are doubled and each CR+LF pair is written as '\n'.

open: The legacy inspector stops with an unhandled error when a presentation item's ID matches no element; what should the person see instead?
Text holding a quote or line break, and lone line feeds in comments, cannot be read back in the legacy program; should the new version escape them or keep this?

title: Choose where to add policy definitions from
what: A person opens the 'add policy definitions' window, chooses where the templates come from, decides whether to clear the loaded definitions first, and then confirms or cancels. Because the product runs in a browser and cannot see the person's folders, the folder choices are replaced by choosing template files (ADMX and ADML) from their own computer.
why: Administrators need to load the right set of policy templates before they can browse or edit any policy, and need a clear refusal when nothing usable was chosen.

terms.name: Policy definitions
terms.means: The administrative template files (ADMX and ADML) that describe the available policies; they are not the policy settings a person has chosen.

terms.name: Clear before adding
terms.means: The option to remove the definitions already loaded before the new ones are added; it is not a deletion of any policy setting.

journey.name: Add policy definitions
steps: Open the window to add policy definitions
Choose where the definitions come from
Pick the template files to add
Decide whether to clear the loaded definitions first
Confirm to add them, or cancel

criteria.says: Given the window has just opened, when the person looks at it, then the choice to pick files from their own computer is already selected, and the file picker and file list are usable.

Given the window is open and another source choice is shown, when the person selects a choice other than picking files from their own computer, then the file picker and file list are not usable, and when they select picking files again, then both become usable.

Given the product cannot reach the person's folders, the Windows folder or a domain's shared policy folder, when the window opens, then no folder or domain choice is offered, and the person can load a domain's definitions only by picking the files they copied from it.

Given the person presses the browse button, when they pick files in their computer's file dialog, then the picked file names appear in the list; and when they close that dialog without picking, then the list is unchanged.
Given the person has picked template files, when they press OK, then the window closes as accepted and those files are the ones added to the loaded definitions.
Given nothing usable has been chosen, when the person presses OK, then they are told what is missing and the window stays open.

Given the window opens, when the person looks at the option to clear the loaded definitions before adding, then it is ticked; and given they press OK with usable files, then their tick or untick is passed on, while given the window was cancelled or refused, then no choice is passed on.
Given the window is open, when the person presses Escape, then the window closes as cancelled and nothing is chosen or added.

open: The old window offered 'the Windows policy definitions folder'; should the new one offer the stored Microsoft package or the installed definitions in its place, or drop that choice?
What exact wording should the refusal show when no files, or no readable template files, were chosen (the old text spoke of a folder that does not exist)?
